extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Official MPEP guidance for examining patent applications and making rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, 112, and related statutes; includes procedural directions (form paragraphs, petition/election rules) and substantive criteria (enablement, written description, obviousness, subject-matter eligibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the invention must come within the statutory classes of 35 U.S.C. 101 (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or improvement thereof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of non-patentable subject matter include mere printed matter, a naturally occurring article substantially unaltered, and bare scientific principles. Use form paragraphs 7.04 through 7.05.03 to reject under 35 U.S.C. 101. The statement of the statute (form paragraph 7.04) must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions on the merits and final rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101) and utility-based rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must have patentable utility; lack of utility includes inoperativeness, perpetual motion, frivolous, fraudulent, or against public policy uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05.02 (utility lacking), 7.05.03 (inoperative) and 7.05.04 (utility + 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph combinations). For 7.05.04 formats, insert whether utility is 'specific and substantial' or 'credible' depending on the factual situation; treat inoperative utilities as not credible. If utility is lacking, also consider enablement (35 U.S.C. 112) and apply In re Wands undue-experimentation analysis per MPEP §§2164-2164.08(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) and determination of prior art date
rubrics_metrics.description: Use form paragraph to reject over a reference (patent or published application) with an earlier filing date that qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e); reference must have common assignee or at least one common inventor when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999, a 102(e) rejection might be overcome by showing the subject matter of the reference and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment at the time the invention was made (see MPEP §706.02(l)(1) and (2)). Apply AIPA-amended 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rules for U.S. patents and U.S. published applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), and for international applications with international filing date on/after Nov 29, 2000. Use pre-AIPA 102(e) only for U.S. patents issued directly/indirectly from international applications filed prior to Nov 29, 2000; consult form paragraph Examiner Notes (e.g., 7.12, 7.12.01) to determine the 102(e) date. Overcoming techniques include showing effective U.S. filing date of the reference under 37 CFR 1.131, submitting an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 that inventor is prior inventor together with a terminal disclaimer per 37 CFR 1.321(c), or proof of common ownership/assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection/use of form paragraphs for 102/103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the correct form paragraph to state the rejection: e.g., do not use the 102(e)-specific form paragraph if the reference qualifies under 102(a) or (b); use 7.21 for 102(a)/(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.22 (further in view of) must be preceded by form paragraph 7.21. Use the Examiner Notes to determine applicable form paragraphs (7.12, 7.12.01, 7.21, 7.22, etc.). Provide a full explanation applying the Graham factors when making 103 rejections; insert appropriate bracketed material (assignee/inventor, explanation of obviousness) as directed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. Deere factual inquiries for obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness analysis requires (1) determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) ascertaining differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (4) considering objective evidence (secondary considerations) indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation of the rejection applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow the form paragraph for an obviousness rejection. Use these four inquiries to structure the factual and legal rationale for a 103 rejection and address any applicant arguments invoking Graham.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of combined 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) rejection (form paragraph 7.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.27 may state a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) or alternatively under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (obviousness) when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended as a common substitute for making a single, specific 102 or 103 rejection; use only in limited circumstances such as: (a) disputed claim interpretation where one interpretation yields 102 and another yields 103; (b) when reference discloses all limitations except a property/function whose inherent presence is uncertain; (c) when a reference teaches a small genus placing a claimed species in public possession; (d) product-by-process situations where product appears same though made by different process; (e) where means-plus-function equivalence is uncertain; (f) overlapping but non-identical ranges where reference lacks specific example within claimed range. Always follow with a full explanation; if relying on 102(e) prior art, determine 102(e) date per AIPA rules as explained in Examiner Notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) applicability for biotechnological processes
rubrics_metrics.description: A biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel and nonobvious under 103(a) shall be considered nonobvious under 103(a) if specified conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements (per statute and MPEP summary): (A) process and composition claims are in the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date; (B) composition and process were owned by the same person or subject to obligation of assignment at the time invented; (C) a patent on the process must also contain the claims to the composition used or made by the process, or if composition is claimed in another patent, the patents must expire on the same date; (D) the process falls within the statutory definition of 'biotechnological process'; and (E) a timely election to proceed under 103(b) is made via petition under 37 CFR 1.182 that establishes all requirements are satisfied. Definition of biotechnological process includes genetic alteration to express/inhibit nucleotide sequences, cell fusion producing a cell line expressing a specific protein (e.g., monoclonal antibody), and methods of using products produced by such processes. Timeliness: election normally by earlier of issue fee payment or filing an appeal brief; certain historical timing exceptions noted (e.g., issue fee paid before Mar 26, 1996).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and rare necessity of relying on 35 U.S.C. 103(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) precludes rejecting process claims that involve use/making of certain nonobvious biotechnological compositions; reliance on 103(b) should be rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP notes Federal Circuit decisions (In re Ochiai, In re Brouwer) suggesting reliance upon 103(b) will be rare because an otherwise conventional process could be patented if limited to making/using a nonobvious product. If a patent issues on a process entitled to 103(b) benefits without an election due to error without deceptive intent, reissue may be filed to permit consideration of qualifying process claims. See 35 U.S.C. 282 for effect on presumption of validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary focus on prior art; development of major non-prior-art rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination should concentrate on patentability over the prior art; non-prior-art or 'technical' rejections should not be given undue emphasis unless truly essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a major technical (non-prior-art) rejection is proper (e.g., lack of proper disclosure, undue breadth, utility), the rejection should be stated with a full development of reasons rather than a mere conclusion with stereotyped expressions. References to where different non-prior-art rejections are discussed: MPEP §§706.03(a), 2105-2107.03, §706.03(b), §§706.03(o), 804, §706.03(s), §706.03(u)-§706.03(x), and §§2161-2174.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.31.01 for rejections under the written-description requirement; precede with form paragraph 7.30.01 (statutory basis). In bracketed explanation identify pages/lines/drawings not supporting the claim, explain examiner's position, include any unresolved examiner questions that raise doubt as to possession. If examiner believes nothing within the claim scope is enabled, use form paragraph 7.31.02 instead and explain why nothing is enabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable one skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.31.02 for enablement rejections; precede with form paragraph 7.30.01. Identify the claimed subject matter for which the specification is not enabling and explain why, applying In re Wands factors (858 F.2d 731) and undue-experimentation analysis per MPEP §§2164-2164.08(c). If the problem is scope versus enablement use form paragraph 7.31.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of enablement (commensurability) — 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (7.31.03)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection where the specification is enabling for some aspects but does not reasonably provide enablement commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.31.03 preceded by 7.30.01. Identify which subject matter is enabled and which aspects the specification does not enable; explain whether the specification enables 'make'/'use'/'make and use' for the scope commensurate with the claims and apply In re Wands factors as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected where the best mode contemplated by the inventor has not been disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.31.04 (preceded by 7.30.01). In bracket 2, insert the basis for holding the best mode has been concealed (e.g., quality of disclosure so poor as to effectively conceal). Use of this paragraph should be rare; see MPEP §§2165-2165.04 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement/critical feature omitted) — 7.33.01
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, where disclosure is not enabling and a feature considered critical or essential by applicant to practice the invention is omitted from the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01. In bracket 2 recite the subject matter omitted from the claims. Examiner must cite applicant statement/argument/drawings or other evidence demonstrating the feature was considered essential by applicant and explain why omission renders the claims non-enabling (see In re Mayhew).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph) — failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention; otherwise they are indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.01 preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02. Follow with one or more specific form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.11 as applicable, or supply a full explanation identifying the particular terms/limitations making claims indefinite and why. If the claim scope can be determined by one of ordinary skill in the art, a 7.34.01 rejection is inappropriate. See §§2171-2174 for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology inconsistent with accepted meaning (applicant as lexicographer) — 7.34.02
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant acts as own lexicographer redefining a claim term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the term to put one skilled in the art on notice of the uncommon definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.02 (preceded by 7.34.01). Identify the term, the meaning assigned by applicant in claim, and the accepted meaning; supply support for examiner's stated accepted meaning (textbook/dictionary). The specification must clearly redefine the term or the term renders the claim indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative term / term of degree rendering claim indefinite — 7.34.03
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a relative term (term of degree) without a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree renders the claim indefinite if one skilled in the art would not be reasonably apprised of scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.34.01. In bracketed explanation specify which parameter/quantity/limitation is rendered indefinite by the relative term and why; provide analysis showing absence of a standard in the claim or specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad range and narrow range/limitation in same claim rendering indefiniteness — 7.34.04
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a broad range or limitation together with a narrower range/limitation that falls within the broad range may be indefinite because it raises doubt whether the narrow language is exemplary or required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.04 (preceded by 7.34.01). Identify the broader range/limitation and the narrower one (insert in brackets) and explain how the inclusion creates indefiniteness. See cited Board of Patent Appeals decisions (Ex parte Wu, etc.) for examples. Modify the paragraph to fit other instances of indefiniteness arising from similar language patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of antecedent basis in the claims — 7.34.05
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a limitation without proper antecedent basis (e.g., introducing an element without previously identifying it) is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.05 (preceded by 7.34.01). In bracketed text insert the limitation lacking antecedent basis and indicate where in the claim it appears; explain why antecedent basis is insufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art of the scope and meaning of the limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic Energy Act restrictions and reporting procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain subject matter useful solely in utilization of special nuclear material or atomic energy in atomic weapons is barred from patenting under the Atomic Energy Act; applications disclosing or appearing to disclose atomic-energy-related inventions must be reported to the Department of Energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See sections 151(a), 151(c)-(d) of the Atomic Energy Act and 37 CFR 1.14(f). Applications are screened by TC work group 3640 personnel and forwarded to Licensing and Review if related to atomic energy; all rejections based upon sections 151(a), 152, and 155 must be made only by TC work group 3640 personnel. Reporting does not constitute determination that subject matter is useful or qualifies under the Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statutory-basis form paragraphs for first actions and final rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory text quotations (e.g., form paragraph 7.04 for 35 U.S.C. 101, 7.30.01/7.30.02 for 35 U.S.C. 112) are required in first actions on the merits and final rejections and are to be used only once in a given Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs quoting the statute are to be used only once in an Office action; if the statute is not re-cited elsewhere in an action on the merits, use paragraph 7.103. Ensure preceding or accompanying statutory-basis paragraphs are included where the MPEP directs (e.g., 7.30.01 must precede 112 first-paragraph form paragraphs).
